distillation_scope: Pure disease-name first-layer leaf distillation for Strongyloides hyperinfection, including accelerated gut-lung autoinfection and context-dependent disseminated complications without splitting by trigger, host, organ, or organism-translocation subtype.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistent Strongyloides stercoralis intestinal infection maintained by autoinfection, often for decades after remote endemic exposure and sometimes with intermittent eosinophilia, mild GI or skin symptoms, or no symptoms.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cellular and Th2 immune control failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Loss of parasite-controlling immunity from corticosteroids, transplant immunosuppression, HTLV-1, hematologic malignancy, advanced HIV, malnutrition, or critical illness; corticosteroids can both suppress eosinophil signals and accelerate larval transformation.

Massive increase in invasive filariform larvae cycling through intestinal mucosa, bloodstream, lung, trachea, and swallowed GI tract; the core organism-burden mechanism reduced by active anti-Strongyloides exposure.

Larval penetration and mucosal inflammation in stomach, small bowel, and colon causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, ileus, malabsorption, protein-losing enteropathy, bleeding, bacterial translocation, and unreliable oral absorption.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pulmonary larval migration and lung injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Heavy larval migration through alveoli and airways causing cough, wheeze, dyspnea, infiltrates, consolidation, hemorrhage, hypoxemic respiratory failure, and ARDS, often with concomitant enteric bacterial sepsis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Enteric bacterial translocation carried by larvae
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Larval mucosal penetration transports gut bacteria across barriers, producing gram-negative, enterococcal, anaerobic, or polymicrobial bacteremia, sepsis, meningitis, pneumonia, and metastatic infection.
Larval spread outside the usual gut-lung autoinfection circuit to CNS, skin, urinary tract, liver, heart, or deep tissues; often coexists with bacteremia or tissue bacterial infection.
Combined parasite burden, lung injury, bacterial sepsis, shock, malabsorption, AKI, coagulopathy, and delayed diagnosis driving short-term mortality.

Filariform larvae migrate through pulmonary circulation and alveoli as part of autoinfection.
Larvae crossing the gut wall create a route for gut organisms into blood and distant sites.

Shock and multiorgan failure strongly lower RMST.

supportive_care: Keep larvae detection in stool, sputum, BAL, gastric aspirate, tissue, CSF, serology, and donor testing as microbiology or confirmatory context; do not delete these data from cases even when a presentation-only ranking mode ignores them.

Screen exposure and host context explicitly: remote tropical/subtropical residence, rural soil exposure, migration, Southeast United States exposure, donor-derived transplant context, corticosteroids, transplant drugs, HTLV-1, HIV, malignancy, malnutrition, and eosinophil history.
Repeat stool and respiratory sampling when suspicion remains because early stool or serology can be negative, especially under immunosuppression.
Track pulmonary severity with respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, P/F ratio, imaging extent, ventilatory support, ARDS hazard, and concurrent bacterial pneumonia or bacteremia.
Track GI severity with diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, ileus, oral absorption reliability, albumin, bleeding or peritonitis signs, and need for nonoral antihelminthic route.

Treat enteric bacterial translocation as a parallel causal pathway: obtain blood cultures, tailor active antibiotics, assess CNS penetration when meningitis is suspected, and re-check for abscess or other source-control needs.
When CNS symptoms occur, preserve CSF profile, cultures/PCR, neuroimaging, ventriculitis, seizure, mental status, and any larval detection separately from final diagnosis text.
If shock or ARDS is present, provide ICU organ support while antihelminthic, antibacterial, route, and immunosuppression-reduction vectors act.
Reduce or stop immunosuppression when feasible, but represent transplant rejection or autoimmune flare as competing context rather than as an external treatment label.

Assess Loa loa risk before ivermectin when epidemiologically relevant, especially for Central or West African exposure, without letting this replace urgent specialist-directed management of severe hyperinfection.
Continue larval-clearance monitoring and adapt route/duration when stool or sputum remains positive or oral absorption is unreliable.

Separate Strongyloides hyperinfection from chronic uncomplicated strongyloidiasis, PJP, bacterial meningitis, bacterial sepsis, transplant pneumonia, and generic ARDS; shared axes are fair, but the accelerated larval autoinfection plus host trigger and gut-lung organism evidence define this leaf.
quality_notes: No treatment ranking-label fields are used.

New axes are limited to medically real Strongyloides-specific larval detection, route, and complication context; shared fever, GI, pulmonary, bacteremia, CNS, shock, and source-control axes are reused where practical.
Strongyloides confirmation, serology, culture species, donor serology, and post-treatment clearance should remain structured but can be marked non-ranking in presentation-only case tests.
